extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing and evaluating elementary mathematical proofs: proving set equalities, methods of disproof (counterexamples, contradiction), and mathematical induction, including common provisos and how to present counterexamples and induction steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving two sets are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that A = B, show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents this directly as the method used to prove A = E (the set equality example). Show both inclusions separately: assume an arbitrary element of one set and prove it belongs to the other, then reverse roles. The example duplicates Euler's reasoning to illustrate this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove a statement by proving its negation (~P)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as the central strategy for disproof: proving the negation immediately shows the original statement is false. In practice you may use direct, contrapositive, or contradiction methods to prove ~P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving universally quantified statements (use a counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a statement of the form ∀x∈S, P(x), produce an x∈S that makes P(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negation of a universal statement is an existence statement (∃x∈S, ¬P(x)). Hence a single explicit example (counterexample) suffices. The text gives the outline: 'Produce an example of an x∈S that makes P(x) false.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving conditional statements by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P(x) → Q(x), produce an x that makes P(x) true and Q(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the conditional fails exactly when there exists an x with P true and Q false, such an example constitutes a counterexample. The text gives the explicit outline for this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and verify counterexamples fully
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting a counterexample, explain exactly how it makes the statement false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that simply naming a counterexample (e.g., 'consider n = 11') is insufficient; you must show the specific reason it fails (e.g., show the factorization f(11)=11·11 so f(11) is not prime). Provide the calculation or reasoning that demonstrates ¬P(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving existence statements (prove universal negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove ∃x∈S, P(x), prove its negation ∀x∈S, ¬P(x) using direct, contrapositive, or contradiction methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since negation of an existence statement is universal, a single counterexample will not suffice; you must prove the property fails for every element of S. The text illustrates using contradiction to show no real x can satisfy x^4 < x < x^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P via contradiction: assume P is true and deduce a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because proving ¬P by contradiction reduces to assuming P and deriving an impossibility, this is a standard technique for disproof. The text presents an outline: 'Assume P is true, and deduce a contradiction,' and works through an example step-by-step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀n∈N, S_n, use induction: (1) prove the basis step (S_1 or appropriate base), and (2) prove the inductive step S_k ⇒ S_{k+1} for arbitrary k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inductive step is usually proved by assuming S_k (the inductive hypothesis) and showing it forces S_{k+1}. The text uses the domino analogy and provides the standard two-step outline and multiple worked examples (sums of odd numbers, divisibility, inequalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and justify the correct base/indexing for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The first statement in an induction proof may be S_1, S_0, S_m, etc.; pick the base suited to the problem and prove it explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the statements are indexed over Z rather than N, you may need to verify a different base and prove forward and backward implications (e.g., show S_a and S_k⇒S_{k+1} and S_k⇒S_{k-1}). The text highlights this when explaining induction over integers versus natural numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction for statements with extra parameters (uniform inductive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving ∀n∈N, P(n,x) where P depends on an additional variable x, the inductive step must show S_k ⇒ S_{k+1} holds for all allowed x simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bernoulli inequality example ((1+x)^n ≥ 1 + nx for x>-1) demonstrates proving the inductive implication 'for all x' by multiplying by a positive quantity (1+x) and handling uniformly the extra parameter. Ensure any algebraic manipulations are valid for the full domain of x used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical induction from inductive (heuristic) reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical induction is a rigorous method proving statements with certainty and should not be confused with inductive reasoning (drawing likely conclusions from examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly warns students about this common confusion and emphasizes induction's certainty versus empirical pattern-spotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic/manipulation cautions used in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating inequalities or divisibility statements, observe sign/positivity and divisibility-preserving operations (e.g., multiply/divide by positive numbers without reversing inequality; removing a positive term makes the side smaller).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: multiply both sides of an inequality by a positive quantity to preserve direction; when proving divisibility by induction, express differences and factor to exhibit an integer multiple. The text points these tactics out in worked induction proofs and inequality manipulations.
